# Compacted Summary: Chapters 1–18 (Complete – Updated 133)

## Setting and Time
- **Current Period**: **Summer of fifth year** (Chapter 18). Spring 1816 events completed. Winter 1815-16 passed. Waterloo campaign: 16 June 1815 morning—regiment receives marching orders; by dawn 17 June—wounded return; 18 June (Sunday)—religious services. **Critical event (26 March 1816)**: Rebecca delivers son (Rawdon minor) and heir to Rawdon. **Spring 1816**: Pitt marries Lady Jane at Brighton; moves into Miss Crawley's house. Lady Southdown assumes control. Miss Crawley dies (spring/early summer 1816). **Late autumn 1815**: Mr. Osborne announces trip to Belgium; church incident with George's monument; confrontation with Colonel Dobbin in Brussels. **Chapter 17 timeline**: Approximately 3-4 years after Paris establishment; Rawdon and Rebecca now in Curzon Street, May Fair, London. **Chapter 17-18 events**: Pitt receives Rebecca's letter (graciously); declines to send £30,000 to Rawdon but offers hand and willingness to serve young Rawdon; nearly reconciliation between brothers. Pitt and Lady Jane absent from London when Rebecca arrives; Miss Crawley's house in Park Lane not yet occupied; Miss Crawley's domestics dismissed with gratuities; French novels sold to bookseller on Bond Street. Engaging society figures: young Lord Southdown, Lord Steyne. **Chapter 18 setting**: Summer, fifth year; river crossing at Quenwick mentioned.
- **Locations**: London (Russell Square, Thames Street, Slaughters' hotel, Gray's Inn Square, Hulker and Bullock bankers, Curzon Street May Fair, Fulham, Park Lane, Bond Street, Bayswater, Hyde Park, opera), Brussels, Belgium, Waterloo battlefield, Brighton, Southampton, Paris, Faubourg St. Germain, Coldcombe hill farms, Dunholt, Calais, Dunkirk, Red Lion Square, Cursitor Street, Tooting, Gulton, Quenwick, Queen's Crawley, Clapham, Sugar-cane Lodge, various other towns.

## Main Characters

**Captain William Dobbin (now Colonel)**
- **Promoted to Major, then Colonel** after second Major's death at Waterloo. Greatly respected. Secret, unrequited adoration of Amelia. **Late autumn 1815**: In Brussels with recovering regiment. **Confrontation with Mr. Osborne**: Pleaded for forgiveness of Amelia and unborn child; complete rejection. **Role**: Brought Amelia back to England to her mother's house in Fulham. **Godfather to Georgy**: Became godfather of infant; purchases gifts constantly. **Chapter 17 status**: Visits Amelia's house daily; experienced crushing realization of hopeless love. Knows no place for him in her heart. Gently bears his fate; content to remain.

**George Osborne**
- **DEAD at Waterloo (16 June 1815, though monument inscription states 18 June)**. Married Amelia late April without father's consent; disinherited. Received £2,000 in 4 percent annuities and £100/year widow's allowance for Amelia. At Brussels: desperate flirtation with Rebecca. **Written final letter before daybreak 16 June** to father (delivered July): farewell before great battle; imploration for Amelia's provision; contrition; thanks. Seal robbed from dead body. **Monument erected** with inscription stating death 18 June, aged 28, "while fighting for his king and country."

**Amelia Osborne**
- **Widow and Mother**. Delivered infant Georgy, godchild to Colonel Dobbin. Status: receives £100/year widow's allowance; holds £2,000 in 4 percent annuities. **Health**: Severely shaken at Waterloo; recovery underway by time Dobbin brought her to England. **Chapter 17 status**: Living with parents in Fulham; fully recovered and devoted entirely to mothering Georgy. Existence is maternal caress; nurtures, dresses, lives upon him. Shows bright maternal pleasure. Laughs when Major arrives; kisses him with hopeless kindness.

**Colonel Rawdon Crawley**
- **Married to Rebecca**. Made last dispositions before campaign. Gallantry mentioned in Gazette; promoted to Lieutenant-Colonel; awarded C.B. **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloo)**: Quitted Guards and sold out. Lived comfortably on "nothing per annum" through gambling and financial ingenuity. **Incident with Colonel O'Dowd**: Violent fracas at Cafe de Paris; nearly challenged; Commander-in-Chief intervened; no duel. **Recent assessment**: Rebecca convinced him gambling income precarious. **Upon Miss Crawley's death news**: Hastily departed Paris; diverted to Dunkirk; owed more money at London than Paris. **Chapter 17-18 status**: Arranging inheritance affairs in London; wife and child followed; occupying furnished Curzon Street, May Fair house without payment. **Character observation**: Plays ecarte with friends; wife has all talk and admiration while he sits silent without comprehending jokes and allusions—wearisome to ex-dragoon.

**Little Rawdon (Son)**
- **Born 26 March 1816**. In Paris: placed out at nurse in village with foster-brothers; nearly drowned on Calais sands through maid's neglect. **London period (Chapter 17-18)**: **Hidden upstairs in garret or kitchen**, scarcely noticed by mother. Passed days with French bonne; when Frenchwoman departed, taken to housemaid's bed in garret by compassionate servant for comfort. **Relationship with father**: Rawdon affectionate and devoted. Maintains private interviews every morning during shaving; boy sits on box watching with pleasure; sweetmeats hidden in old epaulet box for discovery and joy. Father buys picture-books, crammed nursery with toys; walls covered with pictures father purchased and pasted. When off duty, spends hours with boy who rides on his chest, pulls his mustachios as driving-reins, spends days in indefatigable gambols. **Incident**: Once when boy not five years old, father tossing him wildly hit child's skull violently against ceiling, terrified at near-disaster.

**Rebecca Sharp (Mrs. Rebecca Rawdon Crawley)**
- **Paris period (3-4 years post-Waterloo)**: Flourished; merits place of honour in Vanity Fair through wit, talent, energy. **By 26 March 1816**: Delivered son and heir. Wrote letters to Miss Crawley (attributed to Rawdon); sent war relics. **Miss Crawley's discovery and fury**: When fraud discovered, fury "beyond bounds"; repudiated Rebecca as "most artful and dangerous person." Duchess of X misreported as "charming letter" with "benevolent things." **Parisian society success**: Achieved very smart and leading position; welcomed at distinguished houses. **Child care**: After amiable French custom, placed son out at nurse; did not care to visit; once infant spoiled dove-coloured pelisse; preferred nurse's caresses to mamma's.

**Chapter 17-18 status**: **Negotiated creditor debts (COMPLETED)**: Offered creditors ninepence or shilling per pound dividend over fifteen hundred pounds to cover debts exceeding fifteen thousand pounds. Returned reporting "entire liberation." **London society reception**: Speedily became vogue among certain class; demure chariots at door with great people; opera box crowded; wit and cleverness made her fashionable. **Female society rejection**: Ladies hold aloof; doors shut; cut publicly by former friends (Lady Bareacres, Lady de la Mole, Mrs. Blenkinsop). Now attends church regularly with Rawdon, carrying gilt prayer-books. **Letter to Pitt**: Composed gracious letter received by Pitt more graciously than previous compositions; Lady Jane so charmed expected instant division of aunt's legacy. **Pitt's response**: Declined £30,000 cheque but made handsome offer of hand; thanked Rebecca; pronounced willingness to serve little boy. **Expectations for London society**: "When Lady Jane comes, she shall be my sponsor in London society; and as for the women! bah! the women will ask me when they find the men want to see me." **Social activities with Lord Steyne**: Displays herself at gatherings (fresh pink dress, dazzling white arms and shoulders, thin hazy scarf, curls round neck, prettiest little foot in sandal and finest silk stocking). Sings charming French songs, plays piano, charms nobleman with wit. Young Lord Southdown offers suggestions about dogs. Lord Steyne (great nobleman, short, broad-chested, bow-legged, bald with red hair fringe, bushy eyebrows, bloodshot eyes, underhung jaw with protruding buck-teeth, wears garter and ribbon, proud of foot and ankle) attends her gatherings, sometimes sits with Rawdon playing ecarte. **Child neglect observation**: When little Rawdon cries overhead from garret, dismisses matter sardonically; tells Lord Steyne "he'll cry himself to sleep"; did not offer to visit child.

**Mr. Raggles (Former Butler)**
- **Background**: Born on Queen's Crawley estate; son of gardener; rose from knife-board to butler. Served Miss Crawley many years with good wages and perquisites. **Marriage**: Contracted matrimonial alliance with former cook of Miss Crawley; news brought by two children of seven and eight years. **Property and income (Chapter 17-18)**: Purchased house in Curzon Street to let; brought handsome yearly income. Loves and adores Crawley family as source of prosperity. Only decoration addition is print of Queen's Crawley in Hampshire, seat of Sir Walpole Crawley, Baronet. **Current tenant**: Crawleys occupy furnished house.

**Financial Relationship (Chapter 17-18)**
- **Unpaid debts**: Rawdons generously patronize Miss Crawley's tradesmen; some willing, especially poor ones. Washerwoman from Tooting brings cart weekly with unpaid bills. Raggles himself supplies greengroceries. **Nobody paid**: Blacksmith, glazier, jobber, groom, butcher, coals, servants owe greater part of wages. Bills remain outstanding. Example of living "elegantly on nothing a year."

**Pitt Crawley and Lady Jane**
- **Married spring 1816 at Brighton** (hastily arranged by Miss Crawley). Moved into Miss Crawley's house. **Upon Miss Crawley's death**: Inherited substantial legacy. **London movements**: Not in London when Rebecca arrived; made only one appearance to conduct business with lawyers and sell Miss Crawley's French novels to bookseller on Bond Street. Miss Crawley's domestics dismissed with decent gratuities. Lady Jane not yet taken possession of Park Lane house.

**Other Characters**
- **Mr. Osborne (Elder)**: George's father. Placed household in mourning. **Late autumn 1815**: Announced trip to Belgium. In Brussels, sought soldiers, paid guinea for intelligence. Confronted by Dobbin; refused reconciliation completely. Soldiers feasted on his generosity.
- **Mrs. O'Dowd**: Distinguished herself at Waterloo; Major became Colonel and C.B.; received summons forcing quit of Amelia; confronted Rebecca at Cafe de Paris.
- **Sir William Dobbin (Alderman)**: Delivered George's sealed letter to Mr. Osborne.
- **Jos Sedley**: Fled Brussels 16 June toward Ghent. Current status (late autumn 1815): widow Amelia's uncertain source of financial aid.
- **Lord Steyne**: Great nobleman; notorious in early life for daring and success at play; sat two days and nights with Mr. Fox at hazard; won money from august personages; allegedly won his marquisate at gaming-table; dislikes allusions to past fredaines; attends Rebecca's gatherings; sometimes plays ecarte with Rawdon; sits nodding over her piano singing.
- **Young Lord Southdown**: Society figure; offers suggestions about dogs to Rebecca.
- **Other established characters**: Osborne's Sisters, Mr. Clapp, Little Mary (Clapp's daughter), Tom Stubble, Pauline, Isidor, Towzer, Sergeant, James Crawley (Jim), General Tufto, Mrs. Brent, Lieutenant Spooney, Blackstone, Count Punter, Green (Rifles), Colonel O'Dowd, Lady Southdown, Briggs, Bowls, Firkin, Creamer, Rodgers, Mr. Waxy (solicitor), Mademoiselle Genevieve (French bonne), Orrin Stenworth, Cotho Hollwood, Fedette and Nynelle Stenworth, Zanar Hollwood, Halan, Ridan Corrett, Madrek Orlwood. **Minor local figures**: Mentioned briefly in fragmentary scenes (baker's boy, ribbon stall, step-scrubber, lane children, muddy square, water crossing, parsonage lavender, house servants, Dolly the housemaid).

## Critical Facts and Status
- **George's Monument Discrepancy**: Inscription states 18 June 1815; actual death 16 June 1815.
- **Amelia's Complete Recovery**: Fully recovered, devoted entirely to mothering Georgy.
- **Dobbin's Hopeless Love**: Recognizes no place for him in Amelia's heart.
- **Rebecca's London Ascendancy**: Fashionable among certain class; ladies' doors shut; cut publicly; attends church regularly; courted by powerful men like Lord Steyne.
- **Little Rawdon's Neglect by Mother**: Hidden upstairs, cared for by servants; father deeply devoted; mother scarcely notices him.
- **Rawdons' Financial Operation**: Live in furnished Curzon Street house without payment; accumulate substantial unpaid debts while maintaining fashionable appearance; pattern exemplifying "living elegantly on nothing a year."
- **Raggles' Vulnerability**: His prosperity depends entirely on Crawley occupancy and eventual payment.
